title: Register: from group chat to formal email
title_target: asså klart!! den e fett bra nu
goal: Move between registers: read chat and slang Swedish, recognize multiethnic youth speech, and switch to a correct formal email when it matters.
bekal: you can read chat Swedish: dropped subjects, *e*, *nåt*, *iaf*, *lr*, *kmr*
you can understand everyday slang (*fett*, *sjukt*, *schysst*, *keff*, *lugnt*) and recognize words from *förortssvenska*
you can write a polite formal email with *angående*, *ytterligare*, *på uppdrag av* and *Tack på förhand*
wave: Go back to Unit 5: say *asså*, *typ*, *liksom* and *ba* in a sentence each, then write each sentence again as it would appear in a formal text, without the particle.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Gruppchatten
dialogs.intro: Jonas's band, Lågtryck, has a group chat with Yasin, the guitarist, who grew up in Tensta in northwest Stockholm. Dian has been added because she keeps asking to hear the new song. The messages are reproduced exactly as typed.

lines.speaker: Jonas:
lines.text: yo, rep ikväll? kl 19 i lokalen
lines.id: Hey, rehearsal tonight? 7 pm at the space
lines.literal: yo, rehearsal tonight? o'clock 19 in room-the

lines.speaker: Yasin:
lines.text: aa kmr. men blir lite sen, jobbar till sex
lines.id: Yeah, coming. But I'll be a bit late, I'm working till six
lines.literal: yeah coming. but becomes little late, work till six

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: får jag hänga med? vill höra nya låten
lines.id: Can I come along? I want to hear the new song

lines.speaker: Jonas:
lines.text: asså klart!! den e fett bra nu
lines.id: I mean, of course!! It's seriously good now
lines.literal: so-like clear!! it is fat good now

lines.speaker: Yasin:
lines.text: wallah den e sjuk. vi har typ fixat refrängen
lines.id: I swear, it's insane. We've kind of sorted out the chorus
lines.literal: I-swear it is sick. we have like fixed chorus-the

lines.text: haha schysst. ska jag ta med nåt?

lines.text: kaffe iaf. o kanske bullar lr nåt
lines.id: Coffee at least. And maybe buns or something
lines.literal: coffee in-any-case. and maybe buns or something

lines.text: len hon e inte din mamma haha
lines.id: Bro, she's not your mom haha
lines.literal: bro she is not your mom haha

lines.text: lugnt, jag bakar kanelbullar ändå
lines.id: It's fine, I'm baking cinnamon buns anyway
lines.literal: calm, I bake cinnamon-buns anyway

lines.text: du e bäst. ses!
lines.id: You're the best. See you!
lines.literal: you are best. see-each-other!

lines.speaker: Yasin:
lines.text: jalla ses
lines.id: OK, let's go, see you
lines.literal: come-on see-each-other

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: ba så ni vet: jag kommer bedöma refrängen
lines.id: Just so you know: I'm going to judge the chorus
lines.literal: just so you-all know: I come judge chorus-the

notes: **aa kmr** — chat Swedish drops the subject when it is obvious (*kmr* = *[jag] kommer*, *jobbar till sex* = *[jag] jobbar…*) and writes words the way they sound: **aa** is the relaxed, drawn-out *ja* (**ah**), **e** is *är*, **nåt** is *något*, **o** is *och*. Capital letters and full stops are optional; exclamation marks are not.

**Vill höra nya låten** — in speech and chat the front article *den* often disappears before an adjective + definite noun: *nya låten* for *den nya låten*, *gamla huset* for *det gamla huset*. In formal writing, put *den* back.

**Asså** (**AHS-soh**) is *alltså* spelled as it sounds. You met it in Unit 5 as a modal particle: here, at the start, it means “I mean, like, obviously”. **Fett** (literally “fat”) and **sjukt** (“sick”) are intensifiers: *fett bra*, *sjukt bra* = “really good”. *Den e sjuk* = “it's amazing”, with the same flip as English *sick*.

**Schysst** (**hwüst**) — “nice, decent, cool”; also “fair”: *Det var schysst av dig* = “That was decent of you”. It is informal but not slang in any rude sense; people of all ages use it. Its opposite in youth speech is **keff** (“bad, lame”).

**Wallah**, **len**, **jalla** — three words from *förortssvenska*, the multiethnic youth Swedish of the suburbs (see the second section). *Wallah* (“I swear”) and *jalla* (“come on, let's go”) come from Arabic; *len* means “mate, bro”. Jonas, who grew up on Södermalm, doesn't use them himself, but he understands them perfectly — many words have spread to young people across the country.

**Ba så ni vet** — *ba* is *bara* (“just”) shortened. And *jag kommer bedöma* drops the *att* of *kommer att* — very common in speech and chat, still frowned upon in careful writing. The most famous use of *ba* is as a quote marker: *och hon ba: ”Va?”* = “and she was like: ‘What?’”.

grammars.title: Spoken and written forms side by side
body: Many Swedish words have a spoken form that differs from the written one. In chat, people write the spoken form; in formal texts, only the written form is acceptable.
after: Språkrådet, the Swedish Language Council, accepts *mej*, *dej*, *sej* and *dom* in informal writing such as private emails and social media. In anything formal — a job application, a report, an email to a landlord — use *mig*, *dig*, *sig* and *de/dem*.
One trap: chat **sen** can mean *sedan* (“later, then”) **or** *sent* (“late”). *Hörs sen* = “talk later”; *blir lite sen* = “I'll be a bit late”. In standard writing they are two different words.

grammars.title: Slang and filler words
body: These are the words you will hear most from Swedes under forty. Understand all of them; use the ones marked “safe” freely.
after: *Skit* (“crap”) as a prefix is surprisingly common and only mildly rude: *skitbra* is a compliment. On its own, *Skit!* is a swear word, so keep it for the prefix.

Slang ages fast. *Fett* has been around since the 1990s and already sounds a bit dated to teenagers; *najs* and *sjukt* are more current. The safest choices for a learner are *typ*, *lugnt* and *schysst* — they never sound forced.

dialogs.title: Text — Mejlet
dialogs.intro: To prepare for a charity concert, the band needs an extra evening at the rehearsal space. Nobody else wants to write to the booking office, so Dian does — and switches register completely.

lines.speaker: Text:
lines.text: Ämne: Förfrågan om extra repetitionstid
lines.id: Subject: Request for additional rehearsal time
lines.literal: subject: inquiry about extra rehearsal-time

lines.speaker: Text:
lines.text: Hej Annika,
lines.id: Dear Annika,
lines.literal: hi Annika,

lines.speaker: Text:
lines.text: Jag skriver på uppdrag av bandet Lågtryck, som repeterar i lokal 3 på tisdagar.
lines.id: I am writing on behalf of the band Lågtryck, which rehearses in room 3 on Tuesdays.
lines.literal: I write on commission of band-the Low-pressure, which rehearses in room 3 on Tuesdays.

lines.speaker: Text:
lines.text: Vi skulle gärna vilja boka ytterligare en kväll i veckan under perioden 1–30 november, om det är möjligt.
lines.id: We would very much like to book one additional evening a week from November 1 to 30, if possible.
lines.literal: we would gladly want book additional one evening in week-the during period-the 1–30 November, if it is possible.

lines.speaker: Text:
lines.text: Anledningen är att bandet ska spela på en välgörenhetskonsert i början av december.
lines.id: The reason is that the band is playing at a charity concert at the beginning of December.
lines.literal: reason-the is that band-the shall play at a charity-concert in beginning-the of December.

lines.speaker: Text:
lines.text: Vi är naturligtvis beredda att betala ordinarie timpris.
lines.id: We are of course prepared to pay the standard hourly rate.
lines.literal: we are naturally prepared to pay ordinary hour-price.

lines.speaker: Text:
lines.text: Skulle du kunna meddela oss om det finns någon ledig tid?
lines.id: Could you let us know whether any time is available?
lines.literal: would you could inform us if it exists any free time?

lines.speaker: Text:
lines.text: Tack på förhand!
lines.id: Thank you in advance!
lines.literal: thanks on beforehand!

lines.speaker: Text:
lines.text: Med vänliga hälsningar
lines.id: Kind regards
lines.literal: with friendly greetings

lines.speaker: Text:
lines.text: Dian, för bandet Lågtryck
lines.id: Dian, for the band Lågtryck
lines.literal: Dian, for band-the Low-pressure

notes: **Ämne** (**EM-neh**) is the subject line, and **förfrågan** (“inquiry, request”) is a typical formal noun. A good Swedish subject line is short and neutral: *Förfrågan om…*, *Angående…*, *Fråga om faktura 1234*.

**Hej Annika,** — Swedish emails, even formal ones, normally open with *Hej* + first name. This is the *du*-reform at work (Svenska 103, Unit 18): titles and surnames have almost disappeared. *Bästa Annika* is a slightly more formal alternative; *Kära* is for personal letters; *Bäste herr…* is museum Swedish.

**På uppdrag av** — “on behalf of”, literally “on commission of”. **Ytterligare** (**ÜT-ter-lee-gah-reh**) is the formal way to say *en till* (“one more”): *ytterligare en kväll* = *en kväll till*. Formal Swedish has a whole set of these pairs (see the grammar box).

**Anledningen är att…** — “the reason is that…”, a clean, impersonal way to give a reason in writing. **Ordinarie** (**or-di-NAH-ree-eh**) means “regular, standard” and never changes its form: *ordinarie pris*, *ordinarie tider*.

**Skulle du kunna meddela oss** — the hypothetical as politeness from Unit 13. *Meddela* (“inform, let know”) is the formal cousin of *säga till*. **Tack på förhand** — “thanks in advance” — is perfectly normal in Swedish and doesn't sound pushy.

**Med vänliga hälsningar** — the standard sign-off, often shortened to *Vänliga hälsningar* or, in quick emails between colleagues, *MVH*. Between friends: *Hälsningar*, *Kram* (“hug”) or *Hörs!*. The signature line *för bandet Lågtryck* shows on whose behalf you write.

grammars.title: Formal word pairs
body: Formal Swedish does not need different grammar, but it does prefer different words. Swap these in when you write to an authority, a landlord or an employer you don't know.

head: Everyday
Formal
Example
rows: Vi kommer inte, **då** vi är sjuka.
Vi **är i behov av** en större lokal.

after: **Då** meaning “since, as” is a hallmark of formal writing: *Då vi inte har fått något svar, skriver vi igen.* It opens a subordinate clause, so BIFF applies: *då vi **inte har** fått*.

Don't overdo it. Modern Swedish authorities write in *klarspråk* (Unit 6), and a private email full of *erhålla* and *vara i behov av* sounds stiff. One or two formal words, a polite question and a correct sign-off are usually enough.

head: Abbreviation
Full form
English
rows: by the way · as soon as possible

blocks.text: The last three rows also appear in normal writing: *dvs.*, *pga.* and *t.ex.* (“for example”) are standard abbreviations, written with full stops in formal texts. English abbreviations such as *btw*, *asap* and *omg* are widely used in Swedish chat — just pronounced with a Swedish accent.

blocks.title: Choosing the register: a ladder
items: **To an authority** (Skatteverket, a court): *Hej,* · *Jag skriver angående…* · *Med vänliga hälsningar* + full name.
**To a landlord, a booking office, an employer you don't know**: *Hej Annika,* · *Skulle du kunna…* · *Med vänliga hälsningar*.
**To a colleague**: *Hej!* · *Kan du kolla på det här?* · *Tack! / MVH / Hörs*.
**To friends**: no greeting, no capitals, *iaf*, *typ*, *lugnt* · *ses!* · *kram*.

blocks.text: **Förortssvenska** (“suburban Swedish”), also called *multietnisk ungdomssvenska* or, in older studies, *Rinkebysvenska*, is a way of speaking that grew up from the 1980s onward among young people in the multilingual suburbs of Stockholm, Gothenburg and Malmö. Linguists stress that it is **not** “broken Swedish”: its speakers are usually native Swedish speakers who switch to standard Swedish at school or work, just as many English speakers switch between a local dialect and standard English.

items: **Words** borrowed from Arabic, Turkish, Kurdish, Persian, Spanish and other languages spoken in the suburbs.
**A distinct rhythm**: more even, staccato syllables, with less of the standard Swedish melody.
**Looser word order**: the verb-second rule is sometimes skipped — *Igår jag gick till stan* instead of *Igår gick jag till stan*.
**Identity**: it signals belonging to a group, which is exactly why it doesn't sound right from outsiders.

head: Word
Meaning
rows: come on, let's go, hurry up

blocks.title: Recognize, don't imitate
items: You will hear these words in music, films, TV series and on any bus in Stockholm. Understanding them is part of understanding Swedish today.
Using them yourself as an outsider tends to sound like a costume. *Jalla* and *keff* have spread so widely that they are safe; leave *aina* and *len* to those who grew up with them.
Spiral review — back to Svenska 102, Unit 20: you wrote your first polite complaint there. Rewrite it now with *angående*, *då*, *Skulle ni kunna…* and *Tack på förhand*.
